questions.stem: Which of the following is not an intensive property?
explanation_steps: An intensive property does not depend on the amount of matter; an extensive property does.
Temperature, melting point and density are the same for a small or a large sample → intensive.
Mass doubles when the sample size doubles → extensive, i.e. NOT intensive.
Option E would mean A, B and C are not intensive, which is false. Answer: D.
tips: Quick test: imagine cutting the sample in half. If the value halves (mass, volume), the property is extensive.
Ratios of two extensive properties (density = mass/volume) are intensive.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is an extensive property?
explanation_steps: Volume depends on how much matter is present (twice the sample, twice the volume) → extensive.
Boiling point, density, colour and melting point do not depend on amount → intensive. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a fluid at room temperature?
explanation_steps: A fluid is any substance that can flow: liquids and gases are fluids; solids are not.
At room temperature (25 °C): helium is a gas, methanol is a liquid, mercury is a liquid metal → all three are fluids.
Uranium is a solid metal → not a fluid.
So all are fluids except B. Answer: E.
tips: 'Fluid' ≠ 'liquid'. Gases are fluids too.
Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature (textbook G9 p.23).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a fluid at room temperature (25 °C)?
explanation_steps: Nitrogen (gas), bromine, water and ethanol (liquids) can all flow → fluids.
Sodium chloride is an ionic solid (m.p. 801 °C) → not a fluid. Answer: D.

questions.stem: Atomic number of an element is 37. What type of bond does the element form with chlorine?
explanation_steps: Z = 37 → electron configuration 2, 8, 18, 8, 1 → one valence electron → Group 1 (IA), period 5: rubidium (Rb), an alkali metal.
Alkali metals lose their single valence electron easily (low ionization energy) to form Rb⁺.
Chlorine (7 valence electrons, high electronegativity) gains one electron to form Cl⁻.
Transfer of electrons from a metal to a nonmetal gives an ionic bond: Rb⁺Cl⁻. Answer: B.
tips: Metal + nonmetal (large electronegativity difference) → ionic; nonmetal + nonmetal → covalent.
Find the group from the last shell of the electron arrangement.

similar_questions.stem: Element X has atomic number 19 and element Y has atomic number 8. The bond formed between X and Y is:
explanation_steps: X: 2,8,8,1 → Group 1 metal (potassium). Y: 2,6 → Group 16 nonmetal (oxygen).
X loses 1 e⁻ (X⁺), Y gains 2 e⁻ (Y²⁻) → ionic compound X₂Y (K₂O). Answer: C.

questions.stem: The difference between chlorine atom and chlorine ion is
explanation_steps: Cl atom: 17 p, 17 e⁻ (2,8,7), neutral. Cl⁻ ion: 17 p, 18 e⁻ (2,8,8), charge −1.
Size differs: the extra electron increases electron–electron repulsion, so Cl⁻ is larger than Cl.
Charge differs (0 vs −1) and electron configuration differs (2,8,7 vs 2,8,8).
The number of protons (17) is the same – it defines the element.
So A, B and C are differences, D is not. Answer: E.
tips: Forming an ion never changes the number of protons (or the identity of the element).
Anions are bigger than their atoms; cations are smaller.

similar_questions.stem: Which property is the SAME for a sodium atom and a sodium ion (Na⁺)?
explanation_steps: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ removes one electron: radius, electron number, charge and configuration all change.
The nucleus is unchanged: both have 11 protons. Answer: D.

questions.stem: The process of settling down of particles due to the gravity is called_________.
explanation_steps: The textbook: 'The process of settling down the coarse particles due to the effect of gravity is called sedimentation.'
Decantation is the pouring off of the clear liquid after sedimentation; filtration uses a filter; evaporation/distillation use heat.
Answer: E.
tips: Sedimentation (settle) comes first, decantation (pour off) comes second.

similar_questions.stem: Pouring off the clear liquid from above a settled solid without disturbing the solid is called:
explanation_steps: Mechanical transfer of the clear upper liquid without disturbing the settled particles = decantation. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The chemical formula of Aluminum Sulphate is:-
explanation_steps: Ions: aluminium Al³⁺; sulphate SO₄²⁻ (a polyatomic ion).
Criss-cross the charges: 2 Al³⁺ (total +6) balance 3 SO₄²⁻ (total −6).
Brackets are needed around the polyatomic ion when more than one is used: Al₂(SO₄)₃. Answer: A.
tips: Check: (number of cations × charge) must equal (number of anions × charge).
Use parentheses only when you need more than one polyatomic ion (MgSO₄ has none).

similar_questions.stem: The correct formula of calcium phosphate is:
explanation_steps: Ca²⁺ and PO₄³⁻. LCM of 2 and 3 is 6 → 3 Ca²⁺ (+6) and 2 PO₄³⁻ (−6).
Formula: Ca₃(PO₄)₂. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs are isoelectronic? (At.No F=9, Ca=20, Ne=10, Mg=12, O=8, Ar=18)
explanation_steps: Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons.
Only Ar (18) and Ca²⁺ (18) match. Answer: E.
tips: Electrons in an ion = Z − (charge). For anions the charge is negative, so you add.
This exact item appears in the G9 textbook review questions (p.77, Q8).

similar_questions.stem: Which pair is isoelectronic? (Z: Na = 11, K = 19, Cl = 17, S = 16, Ne = 10)
explanation_steps: Electrons: Na⁺ 10, K⁺ 18, Cl⁻ 18, Ne 10, S²⁻ 18.
S²⁻ (18) and K⁺ (18) are isoelectronic. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The atomic mass of two stable isotopes, Cu-63 (69.09%) and Cu-65 (30.91%), are 62.93u and 64.93u respectively. The average atomic mass of copper is.
explanation_steps: Average atomic mass = Σ(fractional abundance × isotope mass).
Contribution of Cu-63 = 0.6909 × 62.93 u = 43.48 u.
Contribution of Cu-65 = 0.3091 × 64.93 u = 20.07 u.
Sum = 63.55 u (4 s.f. from the data). The nearest option is 63.53 u. Answer: B.
tips: The average must lie between the two isotope masses and closer to the more abundant isotope – this eliminates A, C, D and E instantly.

similar_questions.stem: Boron has two isotopes: B-10 (19.9%, 10.013 u) and B-11 (80.1%, 11.009 u). The average atomic mass of boron is:
explanation_steps: Sum = 10.81 u. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The valence electrons of the atom X that forms the ionic compound Na₃X is:-
explanation_steps: Na always forms Na⁺. Three Na⁺ (+3) must be balanced by X³⁻.
X gains 3 electrons to reach an octet → X has 8 − 3 = 5 valence electrons (Group 15, e.g. N in Na₃N or P in Na₃P).
The number of valence electrons is a count, never negative (−3 is the ion's charge/oxidation state, not the valence electrons). Answer: C.
tips: Nonmetal valence electrons = 8 − (magnitude of its ionic charge).
Don't confuse 'valency' or 'charge' (−3) with 'number of valence electrons' (5).

similar_questions.stem: An element Y forms the ionic compound CaY₂. How many valence electrons does an atom of Y have?
explanation_steps: Ca forms Ca²⁺; two Y ions balance +2, so each Y is Y⁻.
Y gains 1 electron to complete its octet → 8 − 1 = 7 valence electrons (a halogen). Answer: D.

explanation_steps: Bronze (Cu + Sn), mild steel (Fe + C), brass (Cu + Zn) and solder (Sn + Pb) are all alloys – homogeneous mixtures.
Iron is a pure element.
Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which one of the following is different from the others?
explanation_steps: Brass, bronze, stainless steel and solder are alloys (mixtures). Copper is an element. Answer: B.

questions.stem: How many atoms of sulphur are present in 1gm of carbon disulfide, CS₂? (At.No C=12, S=32)
explanation_steps: Molar mass of CS₂ = 12 + 2(32) = 76 g/mol.
Moles of CS₂ = 1 g ÷ 76 g/mol = 0.01316 mol.
Each molecule has 2 S atoms → S atoms = 2 × 7.92×10²¹ = 1.58×10²². Answer: C.
tips: Distractor A (7.91×10²²) comes from forgetting a factor/misplacing the power; always finish with ×(atoms per molecule).
mass → moles → particles → atoms: m/M × NA × (atoms per formula).

similar_questions.stem: How many oxygen atoms are present in 2.2 g of CO₂? (C = 12, O = 16)
explanation_steps: Molecules = 0.050 × 6.02×10²³ = 3.01×10²²; O atoms = 2 × 3.01×10²² = 6.02×10²². Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following can best be described as polar covalent molecule?
explanation_steps: Cl₂ and H₂: identical atoms share electrons equally → nonpolar covalent.
KCl and NaCl: metal + nonmetal → ionic, not molecules.
HCl: two different nonmetals; Cl is more electronegative than H, so the shared pair is pulled toward Cl (Hδ⁺–Clδ⁻) → polar covalent. Answer: B.
tips: Polar covalent = two DIFFERENT nonmetals. Same atoms = nonpolar; metal + nonmetal = ionic.

similar_questions.stem: Which molecule contains a nonpolar covalent bond?
explanation_steps: O₂ has two identical atoms → equal sharing → nonpolar covalent.
H₂O, NH₃, HF are polar covalent; NaF is ionic. Answer: C.

questions.stem: What is the molar mass of the gas, when the density of the gas at STP is 2.63 g/l.
explanation_steps: At STP one mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L (22.414 L).
Molar mass = density × molar volume = 2.63 g/L × 22.4 L/mol = 58.9 g/mol (with 22.414 L/mol: 58.95 g/mol).
Answer: B (58.95 g/mol – note the unit should be g/mol, not 'gram').
tips: M = d × 22.4 at STP. More generally M = dRT/P.

similar_questions.stem: A gas has a density of 1.25 g/L at STP. Its molar mass is:
explanation_steps: M = 1.25 g/L × 22.4 L/mol = 28.0 g/mol (e.g. N₂ or CO). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following process requires the highest amount of energy.
explanation_steps: Read the intended processes: A = 1st ionization of O, B = 1st ionization of F, C = 1st ionization of He, D = removal of an electron from Na⁺, i.e. the 2nd ionization of sodium (Na⁺ → Na²⁺).
Approximate values: IE₁(O) ≈ 1314 kJ/mol, IE₁(F) ≈ 1681 kJ/mol, IE₁(He) ≈ 2372 kJ/mol, IE₂(Na) ≈ 4562 kJ/mol.
Removing an electron from Na⁺ means breaking into a stable noble-gas (Ne) core, closer to the nucleus and from a positive ion → very large energy.
Answer: D.
tips: Removing an electron from an ion that already has a noble-gas configuration always costs a huge amount of energy (big jump in successive IEs).
Among neutral atoms, He has the highest first ionization energy.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following processes requires the most energy?
explanation_steps: All are first ionizations. IE increases across a period and decreases down a group.
Ne is a noble gas at the far right of period 2 → highest IE₁ (≈2081 kJ/mol) of the list. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.note: Textbook defines first IE and its trends; successive (2nd) ionization energy is not treated explicitly.

questions.review_flag: Typos in the equations: A should read O(g) → O⁺(g) + e⁻, and D should read Na⁺(g) → Na²⁺(g) + e⁻ (as printed both sides are identical). Key assumes the intended 2nd ionization of Na.

questions.stem: Which of the following species is expected to form hydrogen bonding with itself.
explanation_steps: Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to a small, very electronegative atom (F, O or N) plus a lone pair on a neighbouring molecule.
CaCl₂ and NaH are ionic; ethane has only C–H bonds (not polar enough).
HF has an H–F bond → strong H···F hydrogen bonds between HF molecules (the textbook says strongest in HF). Answer: D.
tips: Remember 'FON': H must be attached to F, O or N.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following forms hydrogen bonds between its own molecules?
explanation_steps: Only NH₃ has H bonded to N (F/O/N). H₂S and HCl: S and Cl are not electronegative/small enough. Answer: C.

Answer: A (e.g. H₂S).
tips: Convert mL to L first (150 mL = 0.150 L).

questions.stem: If potassium and sodium metals are put respectively in beaker A and beaker B containing water, then:-
explanation_steps: Active (alkali) metals react with water to form a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas:
2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂ (beaker A);  2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ (beaker B).
KOH and NaOH are strong bases, so BOTH beakers become basic.
Among the options only 'beaker A will be basic' is true. Answer: A.
tips: Metal + water → base (hydroxide) + H₂ ; nonmetal oxide + water → acid.

similar_questions.stem: Calcium is added to water in beaker X; sulphur trioxide is dissolved in water in beaker Y. Which is correct?

options.B: X becomes basic, Y becomes acidic
options.C: X becomes acidic, Y becomes basic

explanation_steps: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂ → basic.
SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ → acidic. Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following salts are insoluble in water except:-
explanation_steps: Textbook solubility rules: all nitrates are soluble; all ammonium salts are soluble.
CaSO₄ (sparingly soluble), PbSO₄ (insoluble sulphate), CaCO₃ (only Na, K, NH₄ carbonates are soluble), AgCl (insoluble chloride).
NH₄NO₃ is both an ammonium salt and a nitrate → soluble. Answer: E.
tips: Always soluble: Na⁺, K⁺, NH₄⁺ salts and all nitrates.
Common insoluble ones: AgCl, PbCl₂ (cold), BaSO₄, PbSO₄, CaSO₄ (slightly), most carbonates.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following salts is soluble in water?
explanation_steps: Only sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates are soluble → K₂CO₃ is soluble.
BaSO₄, PbSO₄, AgCl and CaCO₃ are insoluble. Answer: C.

questions.stem: What is the H₃O⁺ concentration of a solution that has an [OH⁻] of 1×10⁻⁴ M?
explanation_steps: At 25 °C, [H₃O⁺][OH⁻] = Kw = 1×10⁻¹⁴.
Answer: B (pH = 10, basic).
tips: pH + pOH = 14: pOH = 4 → pH = 10 → [H⁺] = 10⁻¹⁰ M.

similar_questions.stem: A solution has [H₃O⁺] = 1×10⁻³ M. What is its [OH⁻]?
explanation_steps: [OH⁻] = Kw/[H₃O⁺] = 1×10⁻¹⁴/1×10⁻³ = 1×10⁻¹¹ M. Answer: B.

questions.stem: _______ is the amount of heat needed when 1 mole of a solid melts to a liquid at its melting point.
explanation_steps: Fusion = melting. The heat needed to melt 1 mol of a solid at its melting point is the (molar) heat of fusion.
Vaporization = liquid → gas; formation = compound from elements; solution = dissolving; neutralization = acid + base.
Answer: B.
tips: Fusion (s→l), vaporization (l→g), sublimation (s→g).

similar_questions.stem: The heat required to convert 1 mole of a liquid into vapour at its boiling point is called:
explanation_steps: Liquid → gas at the boiling point = vaporization. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A 15.0 ml portion of a solution of 0.20M HNO₃ is titrated with 0.10M NaOH. How many ml of NaOH are required to reach equivalence point?
explanation_steps: HNO₃ + NaOH → NaNO₃ + H₂O (1 : 1).
Moles HNO₃ = 0.20 mol/L × 0.0150 L = 3.0×10⁻³ mol = moles NaOH needed.
V(NaOH) = 3.0×10⁻³ mol ÷ 0.10 mol/L = 0.030 L = 30 mL. Answer: B.
tips: For 1:1 reactions: MaVa = MbVb → Vb = (0.20 × 15.0)/0.10 = 30 mL.

similar_questions.stem: 20.0 mL of 0.15 M H₂SO₄ is titrated with 0.20 M NaOH. What volume of NaOH is needed for complete neutralization?
explanation_steps: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O.

questions.stem: When the temperature of reversible exothermic reaction is increased at equilibrium:
explanation_steps: Exothermic forward reaction: reactants ⇌ products + heat.
Le Chatelier: adding heat (raising T) is a stress; the system absorbs the heat by shifting in the endothermic direction, i.e. backward.
Answer: B (the reverse reaction is favoured, K decreases).
tips: Treat heat as a product for exothermic reactions and as a reactant for endothermic ones, then apply Le Chatelier.

similar_questions.stem: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH < 0, lowering the temperature will:

options.A: shift the equilibrium to the left
options.B: shift the equilibrium to the right

explanation_steps: Heat is a product of the exothermic forward reaction. Removing heat (cooling) shifts equilibrium forward → more NH₃. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The equivalent weight of anhydrous Na₂CO₃ (atomic mass Na=23g/mol, C=12g/mol, O=16g/mol)
explanation_steps: Molar mass of Na₂CO₃ = 2(23) + 12 + 3(16) = 106 g/mol.
Na₂CO₃ behaves as a base that reacts with 2 H⁺ (CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂); equivalently the total cation charge is 2.
Equivalent weight = 106 ÷ 2 = 53 g. Answer: C.
tips: Equivalent mass = molar mass ÷ n, where n = replaceable H⁺ (acids), OH⁻ (bases) or total positive charge (salts).

similar_questions.stem: What is the equivalent mass of phosphoric acid, H₃PO₄? (H = 1, P = 31, O = 16)
explanation_steps: M = 3(1) + 31 + 4(16) = 98 g/mol; replaceable H = 3.
Equivalent mass = 98/3 = 32.7 g. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.note: The textbook limits equivalent mass to acids and bases; Na₂CO₃ is treated as a diacidic base (n = 2).

questions.review_flag: Stem is an incomplete sentence (no question verb); options should be g/equivalent. Textbook only defines equivalent mass for acids and bases.

questions.stem: Calculate the freezing point of a solution containing 2.5 mol of MgCl₂ dissolved in 1000 g of H₂O? (Kf of H₂O = 1.86)
explanation_steps: Molality m = 2.5 mol ÷ 1.000 kg = 2.5 mol/kg.
Colligative properties depend on the NUMBER of solute particles. MgCl₂ → Mg²⁺ + 2Cl⁻ gives 3 particles per formula unit (van 't Hoff factor i = 3).
ΔTf = i × Kf × m = 3 × 1.86 °C·kg/mol × 2.5 mol/kg = 13.95 °C.
(If dissociation were ignored, ΔTf = 1.86 × 2.5 = 4.65 °C → −4.65 °C, option A.)
tips: Freezing point always goes DOWN: answers with + signs (B, D) are impossible.
Ionic solutes: count ions (NaCl → 2, CaCl₂/MgCl₂ → 3, AlCl₃ → 4).

similar_questions.stem: What is the freezing point of a solution of 0.50 mol NaCl in 500 g of water? (Kf = 1.86 °C·kg/mol; assume complete dissociation)
explanation_steps: m = 0.50 mol/0.500 kg = 1.0 mol/kg; NaCl → Na⁺ + Cl⁻ so i = 2.

textbook_ref.note: Textbook formula ΔTf = Kf·m; it stresses dependence on the number of solute particles (p.101, 107) but does not name the van 't Hoff factor.

questions.review_flag: Both −13.95 °C (with dissociation, i = 3) and −4.65 °C (textbook formula ΔTf = Kf·m without i) appear as options. Key uses i = 3 because colligative properties depend on the number of particles; Kf units missing (°C·kg/mol).

questions.stem: As one moves across a period from left to right in the modern periodic table,

options.D: non metallic character of elements decreases.

explanation_steps: Across a period the nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell, so electrons are pulled closer.
Result: atomic radius decreases (A true); ionization energy increases (B false); electronegativity increases (C false); nonmetallic character increases (D false).
Answer: A.
tips: Across a period: radius ↓, IE ↑, EN ↑, nonmetallic character ↑. Down a group: the opposite.

similar_questions.stem: Moving DOWN a group in the periodic table:
explanation_steps: Down a group new shells are added → radius ↑, IE ↓, EN ↓, metallic character ↑. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which acid is different from the others depending on basicity?
explanation_steps: Basicity = number of replaceable (acidic) H⁺ ions per molecule.
Sulphuric acid H₂SO₄, hydrosulphuric acid H₂S and carbonic acid H₂CO₃ each have 2 acidic H → dibasic (diprotic).
Acetic acid CH₃COOH has only 1 acidic H (the –COOH hydrogen); the 3 C–H hydrogens are not acidic → monobasic.
Answer: A.
tips: Count only H atoms bonded to O (or directly to the anion, as in H₂S); H bonded to carbon is not acidic.

similar_questions.stem: Which acid is triprotic (tribasic)?
explanation_steps: H₃PO₄ → 3H⁺ + PO₄³⁻: three replaceable H. Answer: D.

questions.stem: The pressure exerted by one mole of methane in 500 ml vessel at 25 °C, assuming ideal behavior. (R = 0.0821 L·atm/mol·K)
explanation_steps: Ideal gas law: PV = nRT → P = nRT/V.
P = (1 mol)(0.0821 L·atm/mol·K)(298 K) ÷ 0.500 L = 48.9 atm. Answer: C.
tips: Always convert: °C → K (+273) and mL → L before using R = 0.0821.

questions.stem: The industrial manufacture of ammonia is called:
explanation_steps: Ammonia is made industrially from N₂ and H₂ (1 : 3 by volume) at high temperature and pressure over an iron catalyst: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ – the Haber process.
Ostwald → nitric acid; Contact → sulphuric acid; Frasch → extraction of sulphur. Answer: C.
tips: Memory aid: Haber–ammonia, Ostwald–nitric acid, Contact–sulphuric acid, Frasch–sulphur.

similar_questions.stem: Sulphuric acid is manufactured industrially by the:
explanation_steps: SO₂ is oxidized to SO₃ over V₂O₅ catalyst and converted to H₂SO₄ in the Contact process. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct about acid-base indicators?

options.A: They are either weak acids or weak bases.
options.B: They demonstrate the end point of acid-base reaction.
options.C: The color of phenolphthalein in an acidic solution is colorless.
options.D: They change color either by losing or gaining H⁺ ions.

explanation_steps: Indicators are weak organic acids (HIn) or bases whose two forms (HIn and In⁻) have different colours → A and D true.
They are used in titration to show the end point → B true.
Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base (textbook Table 4.2) → C true.
Answer: E.
tips: Textbook Table 4.2: methyl orange pink/yellow, litmus red/blue, phenolphthalein colourless/pink (acid/base).

similar_questions.stem: What is the colour of methyl orange in an acidic solution?
explanation_steps: Methyl orange: pink/red in acid, yellow in base (textbook Table 4.2). Answer: B.

questions.stem: An acidic soil can be beneficially changed in character by the addition of:
explanation_steps: To correct acidity we need a base to neutralize the acid.
CaCO₃ (limestone) is a basic salt: CaCO₃ + 2H⁺ → Ca²⁺ + H₂O + CO₂.
CaSO₄, CaCl₂ and Ca(NO₃)₂ are neutral salts of strong acids – they do not neutralize acidity.
Answer: A (lime, CaO/Ca(OH)₂, would also work). For basic soils the textbook recommends ammonium sulphate.
tips: Acidic soil → add lime/limestone; basic soil → add ammonium sulphate (textbook p.133).

similar_questions.stem: A farmer's soil is too basic (alkaline) for a crop. According to the textbook, which substance should be added?
explanation_steps: An alkaline soil needs an acidic substance. Ammonium sulphate is an acidic salt (textbook p.133).
Slaked lime, limestone, sodium carbonate and wood ash are all basic. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Ionization energy of an atom is strongly influenced by

options.A: The distance of the outermost electrons from the nucleus
options.B: The size of the nuclear charge
options.C: The number of inner electron shells
options.D: The type of electrons to be removed

explanation_steps: Ionization energy depends on how strongly the outer electron is held.
Larger distance (atomic radius) → lower IE; larger nuclear charge → higher IE; more inner shells → more shielding → lower IE;
type of electron (s electrons are held more tightly than p; paired vs unpaired) also matters.
All four factors apply. Answer: E.
tips: Think 'attraction vs. distance vs. shielding'.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following atoms has the LOWEST first ionization energy?
explanation_steps: IE decreases down a group (more shells, more shielding, bigger radius) and increases across a period.
K is lowest in Group 1 of this list and to the left of Mg/Be. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following decreases as the amount of solute particles in a solution increases?
explanation_steps: More solute particles → vapour pressure lowered → boiling point rises (A increases).
Freezing point is depressed (B decreases).
Osmotic pressure increases with concentration (C increases); molality increases (D).
Only the freezing point decreases. Answer: B.
tips: Colligative properties: boiling point ↑, freezing point ↓, vapour pressure ↓, osmotic pressure ↑.

similar_questions.stem: Adding more non-volatile solute to a solution INCREASES all of the following EXCEPT:
explanation_steps: BP, osmotic pressure, ΔTf and vapour-pressure lowering all increase with more particles.
The freezing point itself decreases. Answer: E.

questions.stem: How many grams of K₂CO₃ are dissolved in water to make 600 ml of solution whose concentration is 0.3M? (At.wt K = 39.09 g, C = 12 g, O = 16 g)
explanation_steps: Moles = M × V = 0.3 mol/L × 0.600 L = 0.18 mol.
Molar mass K₂CO₃ = 2(39.09) + 12 + 3(16) = 138.18 g/mol.
Option A (24.84 g) is obtained with K = 39; it is the intended answer. Answer: A.
tips: n = MV (V in litres), then m = n × M. Option C (0.18) is the number of moles, not grams – a classic trap.

questions.stem: The minimum amount of energy required by molecules to undergo a reaction during collision is:
explanation_steps: Collision theory: particles must collide with the correct orientation AND with at least a minimum energy.
That minimum energy is the activation energy (Eₐ). Answer: C.
tips: Catalysts speed up reactions by providing a path with LOWER activation energy.

similar_questions.stem: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by:

options.D: shifting the equilibrium to the right

explanation_steps: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy; it does not change ΔH or the equilibrium position. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Calculate the pH of 0.05M of Ba(OH)₂?
explanation_steps: Ba(OH)₂ is a strong base: Ba(OH)₂ → Ba²⁺ + 2OH⁻.
pH = 14 − pOH = 14 − 1 = 13. Answer: B.
tips: Don't forget the 2 OH⁻ per formula unit (using 0.05 M gives pH 12.7 – the trap option C ≈ 12.6).

questions.stem: Which of the following compounds can be polymerized?
explanation_steps: Addition polymerization requires a C=C double bond that can open up and link to neighbouring monomers.
Vinyl chloride (chloroethene), CH₂=CHCl, has a C=C bond → polymerizes to PVC, –(CH₂–CHCl)ₙ–.
Chloromethane and dichloromethane are saturated; benzene is aromatic and does not undergo addition polymerization.
Answer: D.
tips: Monomers for addition polymers are alkenes: ethene → polythene, chloroethene → PVC, tetrafluoroethene → Teflon, styrene → polystyrene.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following can act as a monomer for addition polymerization?

questions.stem: For the reaction N₂H₄ + H₂O₂ − 640 kJ → N₂ + 4H₂O, how much heat is liberated when 7 moles of H₂O₂ react?
explanation_steps: Textbook convention (G10 Table 5.3, form B): 'reactants − heat → products' means the reaction is exothermic; here 640 kJ is released.
A thermochemical equation must first be balanced (textbook guideline 1). Balancing H and O: N₂H₄ + 2H₂O₂ → N₂ + 4H₂O.
So 640 kJ is released per 2 mol H₂O₂ → 320 kJ per mol H₂O₂.
Heat for 7 mol H₂O₂ = 7 × 320 kJ = 2240 kJ. Answer: A.
(If the unbalanced equation is used as printed, 7 × 640 = 4480 kJ, option C.)
tips: Always balance the equation before using the heat value – the heat belongs to the mole ratio of the BALANCED equation.

similar_questions.stem: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, ΔH = −890 kJ. How much heat is released when 2.5 mol of O₂ is consumed?
explanation_steps: 890 kJ is released per 2 mol O₂ → 445 kJ per mol O₂.
2.5 mol × 445 kJ/mol = 1112.5 kJ. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: The printed equation is not balanced (should be N₂H₄ + 2H₂O₂ → N₂ + 4H₂O). Key uses the balanced equation (2240 kJ); using the equation as printed would give 4480 kJ (option C).

questions.stem: Answer questions 40 to 42 based on the following chemical equation:  HNO₃ + SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ + NO.  The coefficient of SO₂ after balancing the equation is:
explanation_steps: Oxidation numbers: N goes from +5 (HNO₃) to +2 (NO): gain of 3 e⁻ per N (reduction).
S goes from +4 (SO₂) to +6 (H₂SO₄): loss of 2 e⁻ per S (oxidation).
Equalize electrons (LCM 6): 2 N and 3 S → 2HNO₃ + 3SO₂ → 3H₂SO₄ + 2NO.
Balance H and O with water: left H = 2, right H = 6 → add 2H₂O on the left. Check O: 6 + 6 + 2 = 14 = 12 + 2 ✓.
Balanced: 2HNO₃ + 3SO₂ + 2H₂O → 3H₂SO₄ + 2NO. Coefficient of SO₂ = 3. Answer: C.
tips: Oxidation-number method: electrons lost = electrons gained, then balance O with H₂O and H last.

similar_questions.stem: When the equation Cu + HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + NO + H₂O is balanced with smallest whole numbers, the coefficient of HNO₃ is:
explanation_steps: Cu: 0 → +2 (lose 2 e⁻); N: +5 → +2 (gain 3 e⁻). LCM 6 → 3Cu and 2NO.
3Cu + HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + H₂O; N needed = 6 (nitrates) + 2 (NO) = 8.
3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO + 4H₂O. Answer: D.

questions.stem: (Based on HNO₃ + SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ + NO)  The oxidizing agent in the reaction is:
explanation_steps: The oxidizing agent is the reactant that is reduced (gains electrons).
N in HNO₃ is reduced from +5 to +2 (in NO).
So HNO₃ is the oxidizing agent. Answer: A.
tips: Oxidizing agent = gets reduced; reducing agent = gets oxidized. Agents are always REACTANTS (so D and E can be excluded).

similar_questions.stem: In the reaction Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, the oxidizing agent is:
explanation_steps: Cu²⁺ (+2) is reduced to Cu (0) → CuSO₄ is the oxidizing agent. Zn is oxidized (reducing agent). Answer: B.

questions.stem: (Based on HNO₃ + SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ + NO)  The reducing agent is:
explanation_steps: The reducing agent is the reactant that is oxidized (loses electrons).
S in SO₂ is oxidized from +4 to +6 (in H₂SO₄).
So SO₂ is the reducing agent. Answer: B.
tips: H₂O takes part only to balance H and O – no oxidation-number change (H +1, O −2 on both sides).

similar_questions.stem: In the reaction 2H₂S + SO₂ → 3S + 2H₂O, the reducing agent is:
explanation_steps: S in H₂S goes from −2 to 0 (oxidized) → H₂S is the reducing agent.
S in SO₂ goes from +4 to 0 (reduced) → SO₂ is the oxidizing agent. Answer: A.

questions.stem: Which of the following molecules has a trigonal pyramidal structure?
explanation_steps: NH₃: N has 3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair → electron-pair geometry tetrahedral; molecular shape trigonal pyramidal (H–N–H ≈ 107°).
CH₃Cl: 4 bonding pairs → tetrahedral. H₂O: 2 bonding + 2 lone pairs → bent. BF₃: 3 bonding pairs, no lone pair → trigonal planar.
Answer: A.
tips: VSEPR: count electron pairs on the central atom; lone pairs occupy positions but are 'invisible' in the molecular shape.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following molecules is bent (V-shaped)?
explanation_steps: H₂O: 2 bonding pairs + 2 lone pairs on O → bent (≈104.5°). CO₂ and BeCl₂ are linear. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The substance with the molecular formula CH₂O is:
explanation_steps: CH₂O is H–CHO, methanal (formaldehyde): a carbonyl group C=O bonded to H.
An aldehyde has the –CHO group on a terminal carbon. Methanal is the simplest aldehyde.
Esters, acids need 2 O atoms; the smallest alcohol (CH₃OH) and ether (CH₃OCH₃) have more H. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: The compound CH₃COCH₃ belongs to the family of:

questions.stem: Which type of crystal has the lowest melting point?
explanation_steps: Molecular crystals (e.g. ice, solid neon, iodine) are held together only by weak intermolecular forces (van der Waals, hydrogen bonds).
Ionic (strong electrostatic attraction), covalent network (covalent bonds throughout, e.g. diamond) and metallic crystals need much more energy to melt.
Answer: C.
tips: Order of melting points (typical): covalent network > ionic ≈ metallic > molecular.

similar_questions.stem: Diamond, which is very hard and has a very high melting point, is an example of a(n):
explanation_steps: In diamond every C atom is covalently bonded to four others throughout the crystal → covalent/macromolecular crystal. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Under what conditions would a gas be expected to behave most ideally?
explanation_steps: Ideal-gas assumptions: negligible molecular volume and no intermolecular attractions.
Low pressure → molecules far apart, so their own volume is negligible.
High temperature → high kinetic energy, so attractions are negligible.
Answer: A.
tips: Real gases deviate most at low T and high P (near liquefaction).

similar_questions.stem: A real gas deviates MOST from ideal behaviour at:

questions.stem: A gas occupying a volume of 450 mL at a pressure of 0.960 atm is allowed to expand at constant temperature until its pressure becomes 0.540 atm. What is its final volume in ml?

questions.stem: The force of attraction between two HCl molecules is;
explanation_steps: HCl is a polar molecule (Hδ⁺–Clδ⁻) with a permanent dipole.
Between two polar molecules the characteristic attraction is dipole–dipole (δ+ end of one attracts δ− end of the other).
Ion–dipole needs ions; dipole–induced dipole is polar + nonpolar (textbook example HCl and H₂); dispersion forces exist too but are not the best description.
Answer: B.
tips: Polar–polar → dipole–dipole; polar–nonpolar → dipole–induced dipole; nonpolar–nonpolar → dispersion; H–F/O/N → hydrogen bond.

questions.stem: Which of the following organic compounds is a saturated hydrocarbon?
explanation_steps: Saturated hydrocarbons contain only C–C single bonds; open-chain ones are alkanes, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
C₃H₈: n = 3 → 2(3)+2 = 8 ✓ → propane, saturated.
C₂H₂ and C₃H₄ (alkynes, CₙH₂ₙ₋₂), C₆H₆ (benzene, aromatic), C₅H₁₀ (alkene CₙH₂ₙ) are unsaturated.
Answer: D.
tips: Fit the formula: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ alkane, CₙH₂ₙ alkene (or cycloalkane), CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ alkyne.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is an unsaturated hydrocarbon?
explanation_steps: C₂H₄ fits CₙH₂ₙ → ethene, which has a C=C double bond (unsaturated). The rest fit CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The maximum amount of solute that can be dissolved in a specified amount of solvent at a given temperature is ____________.
explanation_steps: Solubility is the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in a given amount (usually 100 g or 100 mL) of solvent at a stated temperature.
Concentration is the amount of solute in ANY solution (not necessarily the maximum). Answer: C.
tips: Solubility is always quoted with a temperature, e.g. NaCl 35.9 g/100 mL water at 25 °C.

similar_questions.stem: A solution that contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a given temperature is called:
explanation_steps: At the solubility limit the solution is saturated; more solute will not dissolve. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which one of the following polymers is formed by addition polymerization?
explanation_steps: Addition polymers form from alkene monomers with no small molecule eliminated.
Teflon = poly(tetrafluoroethene), –(CF₂–CF₂)ₙ–, from CF₂=CF₂ → addition polymer.
Nylon and polyester (synthetic fibres), Bakelite and urea–methanal (thermosets) are condensation polymers (water or another small molecule is eliminated).
Answer: C.
tips: Textbook: thermoplastics (polythene, PVC, polystyrene, Teflon) → addition; thermosets and fibres (Bakelite, urea-methanal, nylon, polyester) → condensation.

similar_questions.stem: Which polymer is formed by condensation polymerization?
explanation_steps: Nylon is formed from a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid with elimination of water → condensation. The others come from alkenes (addition). Answer: D.

questions.stem: The rate of chemical reaction increases with:-

options.C: increase in temperature in exothermic reaction.

explanation_steps: Smaller particle size = larger surface area exposed → more collisions per second → faster reaction. A is correct.
B is the opposite of A (smaller surface area slows the reaction). D: an inhibitor (negative catalyst) slows the reaction. E contains B → wrong.

Option C is ALSO correct scientifically: raising the temperature increases the rate of ALL reactions, exothermic or endothermic (the textbook states explicitly that whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic is not the key factor; activation energy is).
Keyed answer: A (the unambiguous statement). A student choosing C is also scientifically right.
tips: Temperature affects RATE (always faster when hotter) and EQUILIBRIUM POSITION (exothermic shifts back when hotter). Don't mix them up.
Rate increases with: higher temperature, higher concentration/pressure, larger surface area (smaller particles), catalyst.

similar_questions.stem: Which change will NOT increase the rate of reaction between marble chips and hydrochloric acid?
explanation_steps: Larger chips have a smaller total surface area → fewer collisions → slower reaction.

questions.stem: If a gas expands at constant temperature,

options.A: The number of molecules of the gas decrease
options.B: The kinetic energy of the molecules increase
options.C: The kinetic energy of the molecules decrease
options.D: The pressure of the gas decreased
options.E: The pressure of the gas remains constant

questions.stem: State the postulates in kinetic molecular theory of gases. (3 pts)
questions.answer:
1. A gas consists of a very large number of tiny particles (molecules/atoms) that are far apart; the actual volume of the particles is negligible compared with the volume of the container.
2. Gas particles are in constant, rapid, random, straight-line motion.
3. Collisions of gas particles with each other and with the walls of the container are perfectly elastic (no loss of total kinetic energy); collisions with the walls cause gas pressure.
4. There are no attractive or repulsive forces between gas particles (except during collisions).
5. The average kinetic energy of the gas particles is directly proportional to the absolute (Kelvin) temperature; at the same temperature all gases have the same average kinetic energy.
explanation_steps: Write each postulate as a separate numbered statement.
Cover: particle size/spacing (negligible volume), motion (constant, random, straight line), elastic collisions, no intermolecular forces, KE ∝ absolute temperature.
Any three correct postulates earn full marks (1 pt each).
marking_points: Award max 3 pts for any three correct postulates
tips: Link each postulate to an observation: negligible volume → gases are compressible; random motion → diffusion; KE ∝ T → pressure rises on heating.
These postulates describe an IDEAL gas; real gases deviate at high P and low T because postulates 1 and 4 fail.

similar_questions.stem: Use the kinetic molecular theory to explain (a) why a gas exerts pressure and (b) why the pressure of a gas in a closed rigid container rises when it is heated.
similar_questions.answer: (a) Gas molecules move constantly and randomly and collide with the container walls; each collision exerts a force, and the total force per unit area is the pressure. (b) Heating raises the average kinetic energy (KE ∝ T), so molecules move faster, hit the walls more often and harder → greater force per unit area → higher pressure (volume constant).
explanation_steps: Identify the relevant postulates: constant random motion; collisions with walls; KE ∝ absolute temperature.
Apply them: more frequent and more forceful collisions = higher pressure.

questions.stem: What mass of copper will be deposited at the cathode by passing a current of 7.89 A for 1200 s through CuSO₄ solution? (F = 96500 C, Cu = 63 g/mol) (3 pts)
explanation_steps: Cathode reaction: Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s)  → Z = 2 electrons per Cu atom.
Quantity of charge: Q = I × t = 7.89 A × 1200 s = 9468 C.
Moles of electrons = Q/F = 9468 C ÷ 96500 C/mol = 0.09811 mol e⁻.
Mass of Cu = 0.04906 mol × 63 g/mol = 3.09 g.
Same result with the textbook formula m = (A/(Z·F)) × I × t = (63/(2 × 96500)) × 7.89 × 1200 = 3.09 g (3 s.f., limited by 7.89 A).
tips: Write the electrode half-equation first – it gives Z (the number of electrons).
Equivalent mass = A/Z = 63/2 = 31.5 g; m = Eq. mass × I × t / F.

questions.stem:
The solubility of Ca(OH)₂ and NaOH at different temperatures in 100 g of H₂O:
Temperature: 10 °C | 15 °C | 20 °C | 25 °C
Ca(OH)₂: 17.5 g | 37 g | 74 g | 148 g
NaOH: 10 g | 25 g | 40 g | 60 g
From the data given calculate:
A. The amount of crystal formed by cooling a saturated solution of NaOH from 25 °C to 15 °C. (1 pt)
B. The molarity and normality of Ca(OH)₂ at room temperature. (density: Ca(OH)₂ = 2.0 g/mL, H₂O = 1 g/mL; Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1 g/mol) (4 pts)
C. Which of the two bases is more soluble at 15 °C? (1 pt)
D. Amount of 2 M H₃PO₄ required to titrate a saturated solution of NaOH at 20 °C. (density NaOH = 2 g/mL) (3 pts)
questions.answer: A. 35 g of NaOH crystals (per 100 g water).  B. At 25 °C: 11.5 M and 23.0 N (if room temperature is taken as 20 °C: 7.30 M, 14.6 N).  C. Ca(OH)₂ (37 g > 25 g per 100 g water, according to the given data).  D. 0.333 mol H₃PO₄ = 167 mL of 2 M H₃PO₄.

subparts.label: A
subparts.question: Crystals formed on cooling saturated NaOH from 25 °C to 15 °C
steps: Solubility at 25 °C = 60 g/100 g H₂O; at 15 °C = 25 g/100 g H₂O.
On cooling, the excess comes out as crystals: 60 g − 25 g = 35 g (from 160 g of saturated solution containing 100 g water).

subparts.label: B
subparts.question: Molarity and normality of Ca(OH)₂ at room temperature
steps: Room temperature = 25 °C (textbook convention) → 148 g Ca(OH)₂ dissolved in 100 g H₂O.
Volume of solution (volumes assumed additive, using the given densities): V = 148 g ÷ 2.0 g/mL + 100 g ÷ 1 g/mL = 74 mL + 100 mL = 174 mL = 0.174 L.
Molarity = 2.00 mol ÷ 0.174 L = 11.5 mol/L (11.49 M).
Ca(OH)₂ has 2 OH⁻ per formula unit → equivalent mass = 74/2 = 37 g → equivalents = 148/37 = 4.00 eq.
If 20 °C is taken as room temperature: 74 g → 1.00 mol; V = 37 + 100 = 137 mL; M = 7.30 M; N = 14.6 N.

subparts.label: C
subparts.question: More soluble base at 15 °C
steps: At 15 °C: Ca(OH)₂ = 37 g/100 g water, NaOH = 25 g/100 g water → Ca(OH)₂ is more soluble according to the table.
(In reality NaOH is far more soluble than Ca(OH)₂; the data in the table are fictitious.)

subparts.label: D
subparts.question: Volume of 2 M H₃PO₄ to titrate saturated NaOH at 20 °C
subparts.answer: 0.333 mol H₃PO₄, i.e. 167 mL (0.167 L) of 2 M H₃PO₄
steps: At 20 °C the saturated solution contains 40 g NaOH in 100 g water → n(NaOH) = 40 g ÷ 40 g/mol = 1.00 mol.
Volume of this solution = 40 g ÷ 2 g/mL + 100 mL = 120 mL → [NaOH] = 1.00 mol ÷ 0.120 L = 8.33 M.
Complete neutralization: H₃PO₄ + 3NaOH → Na₃PO₄ + 3H₂O → n(H₃PO₄) = 1.00 ÷ 3 = 0.333 mol.
V(H₃PO₄) = 0.333 mol ÷ 2 mol/L = 0.167 L = 167 mL.
Check with normality: N(acid) = 3 × 2 = 6 N; NaVa = NbVb → Va = (8.33 N × 120 mL) ÷ 6 N = 167 mL ✓.

explanation_steps: See the sub-part solutions. Key ideas: crystals formed = solubility difference; molarity = moles solute / litres of solution (volume from the given densities); normality = molarity × number of OH⁻; titration uses the 3 : 1 NaOH : H₃PO₄ mole ratio.
marking_points: D: mol NaOH = 1.00 (1), 3:1 ratio → 0.333 mol H₃PO₄ (1), 167 mL (1)
tips: Solubility is per 100 g of WATER, not per 100 g of solution.
When densities of solute and solvent are given, the examiner expects V(solution) = V(solute) + V(water).
H₃PO₄ is triprotic: 1 mol H₃PO₄ neutralizes 3 mol NaOH (normality = 3 × molarity).

questions.stem: Explain the factors affecting the preferential discharge of an ion at an electrode during electrolysis. (3 pts)
questions.answer:
1. Position of the ion in the electrochemical (activity) series: cations of less active metals (e.g. Cu²⁺, Ag⁺, H⁺ before Na⁺) are discharged more readily at the cathode; at the anode, anions lower in the series (OH⁻ before I⁻, Br⁻, Cl⁻, NO₃⁻, SO₄²⁻) are discharged more readily.
2. Relative concentration of the ions: a much more concentrated ion can be discharged in preference to one that is normally preferred – e.g. in concentrated NaCl(aq), Cl⁻ is discharged at the anode (giving Cl₂) instead of OH⁻.
3. Nature of the electrodes: inert electrodes (Pt, graphite) do not take part, but active electrodes can react or favour certain ions – e.g. with a copper anode in CuSO₄(aq) the anode itself dissolves (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻) instead of OH⁻ being discharged; with a mercury cathode Na⁺ is discharged instead of H⁺.
explanation_steps: State the three factors named in the textbook: position in the electrochemical series, concentration, nature of the electrode.
Explain each with one example (1 pt each).
tips: Use NaCl(aq) as your example: dilute → O₂ at anode; concentrated → Cl₂ at anode (concentration effect).
Cathode order (least → most readily discharged): K⁺, Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺, Pb²⁺, H⁺, Cu²⁺, Ag⁺.

similar_questions.stem: Concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed using inert (graphite) electrodes. Name the products at the cathode and at the anode and explain each choice.
similar_questions.answer: Cathode: hydrogen gas – H⁺ (from water) is lower in the electrochemical series than Na⁺, so it is preferentially discharged: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. Anode: chlorine gas – although OH⁻ is normally preferred, the high concentration of Cl⁻ makes it discharge: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. The solution left becomes NaOH.
explanation_steps: Cations present: Na⁺, H⁺ → electrochemical series decides → H₂.
Anions present: Cl⁻, OH⁻ → concentration decides → Cl₂.

questions.stem: Define (3 pts):  A. metallurgy   B. Roasting   C. calcination
questions.answer:
A. Metallurgy: the science and technology of extracting (separating) metals from their ores (including concentration, reduction and refining).
B. Roasting: strongly heating a (sulphide) ore in the presence of excess air to convert it into the metal oxide, e.g. 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂.
C. Calcination: strongly heating a (carbonate) ore in a limited supply of air (or absence of air) to decompose it into the metal oxide, e.g. ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂.
explanation_steps: Use the textbook definitions (G11 p.124 and p.127).
Key distinction: roasting = sulphide ore + EXCESS air; calcination = carbonate ore + LIMITED air; both give the oxide, which is then reduced (e.g. by carbon).
marking_points: Roasting: sulphide ore heated in excess air → oxide (1)
Calcination: carbonate ore heated in limited air → oxide (1)
tips: Roasting → SO₂ released (sulphide ores); calcination → CO₂ released (carbonate ores).

Calcination: thermal decomposition of the carbonate.
Reduction: carbon removes oxygen from the oxide.

subparts.label: A
subparts.question: Mass defect (Δm)
subparts.answer: Δm = −7.5×10⁻²⁷ g = −7.5×10⁻³⁰ kg (mass defect of 7.5×10⁻²⁷ g)
steps: Mass of reactants = 1.6726×10⁻²⁴ g + 1.6749×10⁻²⁴ g = 3.3475×10⁻²⁴ g.
Δm = mass of product − mass of reactants = 3.34×10⁻²⁴ g − 3.3475×10⁻²⁴ g = −0.0075×10⁻²⁴ g = −7.5×10⁻²⁷ g.

subparts.label: B
subparts.question: Binding energy in joules
steps: ΔE = Δm c² = (−7.5×10⁻³⁰ kg)(3.00×10⁸ m/s)² = −6.75×10⁻¹³ J (negative = energy released).
Binding energy = 6.75×10⁻¹³ J (≈ 6.8×10⁻¹³ J; 1 J = 1 kg·m²/s²).

explanation_steps: See sub-parts. Textbook convention: Δm = mass of products − mass of reactants (negative when mass is lost), ΔE = Δm c² with c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s.
marking_points: A: correct subtraction and Δm = 7.5×10⁻²⁷ g (sign may be negative per textbook convention) (1)
B: convert to kg and E = 6.75×10⁻¹³ J (1)
tips: Convert grams to kilograms before using E = mc² (1 g = 10⁻³ kg) so that the energy comes out in joules.
The sign of Δm (negative) just means mass is lost; the binding energy is quoted as a positive quantity.
